How do I decide which job to take first?

Having more work available than weeks to do it in is a good problem, right up until you have to pick. The list on the whiteboard is all real work, all of it wants doing, and the honest answer to “is this a good job?” is yes for nearly every line on it. That question is the wrong one. The one that has an answer is which of these two would I rather have started?

Open the free job priority ranker

Why the scoring sheet does not help

The standard advice is to score each job on margin, effort and risk, add the columns up and sort. It sounds rigorous and it usually produces a column of sevens and eights.

The scale drifts as you use it. Whatever a 7 meant on the first job, it does not mean the same thing by the seventh, because there is nothing holding it in place. You are rating each job against a standard that lives only in your head and has been moving all the way down the page.

Everything worth taking scores well. If a job were obviously bad it would not be on the list. So the scores cluster, the differences between them are inside the noise of your own rating, and the sorted result is close to arbitrary.

The trade-offs are the whole point and scoring hides them. A job that pays well but is ninety minutes away, against one that pays less and is round the corner — that comparison is a real judgement with a real answer. Splitting it into two numbers on separate rows throws away exactly the thing you were trying to decide.

Compare two at a time instead

Pairwise comparison inverts the problem. Instead of asking what a job is worth in the abstract, you hold two of them side by side and answer one question: which would you rather have started? You do not have to explain the answer or break it into factors. Margin, travel, cash timing, crew fit and how much the client will cost you in phone calls all fold into a single preference, which is the form your experience is actually stored in.

Do enough of those and an order emerges. The trick is doing far fewer than every possible pair: twelve jobs have sixty-six pairs, which nobody is going to sit through. A merge sort gets the same twelve into order in roughly thirty-four questions, because once it knows a job sits above a group it stops asking about the rest of that group. Eight jobs take about twenty-two questions; twenty-five take about ninety.

You can run this on paper with index cards. The ranker on this site runs it in the browser, keeps count, lets you undo a misclick, and saves an unfinished run so a phone call does not cost you the progress.

What is really deciding it

You do not need to weight these, and the method above works precisely because you do not have to. But it helps to know what tends to be doing the work when you pick, so you can notice when one of them is quietly running the whole show:

  • Margin per day on site, not margin per job. A $9,000 job over eight days and a $4,000 job over three days are not in the order the totals suggest.
  • When the money lands. A deposit up front against net-30 on completion is a different job to your bank account, whatever the invoice says.
  • Travel and mobilisation. Two hours of driving and a setup is most of a chargeable morning, every day the job runs.
  • What the weather and the calendar allow. Exterior work has a season; some jobs can wait for it and some cannot.
  • What is blocked anyway. A job waiting on a permit, a survey or a long-lead part is not a candidate for next week however good it is.
  • Who the client is. Chasing, scope creep and rework are real costs that never appear on the quote.
  • What it leads to. A small job for a builder who has ten more is not the same as a one-off, and both of them look identical on a scoring sheet.

A worked example

Five jobs on the board. Scored out of ten they would all land between 6 and 8, which is why the sheet does not help. Compared in pairs, the picture separates quickly:

JobValueDaysNotes
Ross kitchen rewire$4,2004Deposit paid, client ready
Mill St deck rebuild$9,5009Waiting on a permit
Cedar fence, 40 ft$2,6002Round the corner
Bathroom retile, Hill Rd$5,1006Net 30, 50 minutes away
Garage door opener$7000.5Repeat client, sends referrals

Asked head to head, the deck loses to almost everything despite being the biggest number, because it cannot start. The fence beats the retile on margin per day and travel even though it is half the money. The opener beats nothing on value and still gets done early, because half a day for a client who keeps sending work is cheap. An order like opener, Ross, fence, retile, deck comes out of five or six comparisons, and it is defensible in a way the scoring sheet never was: every step of it is a preference you stated.

The point is not that these figures are yours. It is that the order is not the order of the values in column two, and no amount of staring at column two would have told you that.

When an order is not the answer

Ordering assumes the constraint is your time and that you are free to choose. Sometimes it is not. If everything on the list is profitable and the list keeps growing, the problem is capacity, and the decisions worth making are about subcontracting, a second crew, or raising prices until the list stops growing — not about sequencing. If two jobs at the bottom have been at the bottom for three months, they are not last; they are declined, and telling the client so is a kindness. An order is also not a commitment: a hard date or a promise you already made overrides it, and it should.

Common questions

How do I decide which job to take first?

Stop trying to rate each job on its own and compare them two at a time instead. Write down every job you could take in the next few weeks, then repeatedly ask yourself one question: of these two, which would I rather have started? Each answer is a judgement you can actually make, because you are weighing two concrete jobs against each other rather than against an imaginary standard. The order falls out of the answers. The free ranker on this site runs that process for you and stops as soon as the order is settled.

Why does scoring each job out of ten not work?

Because the scale drifts while you use it. By the time you reach the seventh job you are scoring against a standard that has already moved from where it was on the first, and there is nothing to anchor it. The usual result is a column of sevens and eights that tells you nothing, so you end up picking by gut anyway after doing the paperwork. Comparing a pair has no scale to drift: you either want that job started before this one or you do not.

What should actually decide the order of my jobs?

Whatever you would be unhappy to have got wrong in six weeks. In practice that is usually margin per day on site rather than margin per job, when the money lands relative to when you pay for materials, how much of a day travel and setup eat, whether the work fits the crew and the weather you have now, what is already blocked waiting on a permit or a supplier, and how much a given client costs you in chasing and rework. You do not have to write these down or weight them. Holding two jobs side by side is what lets you feel the trade-off between them in one judgement.

How many comparisons does it take to order a list of jobs?

Far fewer than every possible pair. Ordering twelve jobs by comparing all of them against each other would take sixty-six questions; a merge sort settles the same twelve in about thirty-four, because once it knows a job beats one group it never asks about that group again. Eight jobs take roughly twenty-two questions and twenty-five jobs take about ninety. That is a coffee break, not an afternoon.

What if the finished order looks wrong to me?

Treat that as the useful part rather than as a failure. A ranking assembled from your own answers can only look wrong if some of those answers disagreed with each other, and the usual reason is a factor you had not admitted was driving you — a client you do not want to work for again, or a job you keep deferring because you are not sure you priced it right. Finding that out is worth more than the list. Move the job by hand and note why.

Should I always work the list in order?

No. An order tells you what to start next when you are free to choose, and there are good reasons not to be: a job with a hard date, a customer you have already promised, weather that suits one job this week and not the next, or a crew that can run two small jobs in the time one big one takes. Use the order as the default and override it deliberately. The value is in having a default at all, so that the overriding is a decision instead of the whole process.

    Common questions

    Why answer this-or-that questions instead of just scoring each job?

    Because scoring a job on its own is a question nobody can answer consistently. Given twelve jobs and a 1-to-10 box, the seventh one gets scored against a standard that has already drifted from the first, and the result is a list of near-identical numbers. A head-to-head question is different: you are comparing two concrete jobs against each other, with every trade-off you care about — margin, travel, how the client pays, whether it fits the crew you have next week — folded into one judgement you can actually make. The ranking is assembled from those answers rather than asked for directly.

    How many questions will it ask me?

    About n times log2 of n, so roughly 22 questions for 8 jobs, 34 for 12, and 90 for 25. The counter above the buttons shows the estimate and how far through it you are. It is a ceiling rather than a promise — the sort stops asking about a group as soon as the answer is settled, so most runs finish a little early, and none run long.

    What happens if I contradict myself?

    You will still get a complete ranking, but it may not be the one you would have described. The method assumes that preferring A to B and B to C means you prefer A to C, and it relies on that to avoid asking about every possible pair — which is what keeps the question count to a few dozen instead of a few hundred. If your answers disagree with each other, the result reflects the order the questions happened to come in. If a finished ranking looks wrong to you, that disagreement is the useful signal: it usually means a job has a factor you had not admitted to yourself, not that the list is unrankable.

    Does my job list leave my browser?

    No. There is no account, no server, and no analytics vendor. Your list and your answers are held in this browser, and an unfinished ranking is saved to this browser's local storage so closing the tab does not lose your progress. Nothing is uploaded at any point.

    What does the share link contain?

    Your list of jobs, encoded after the # in the address — and not your answers or your ranking. A browser never sends the part after # to a server, so pasting that link into a text or an email is the only way it travels. Sending the list rather than the result is deliberate: it lets a partner or a foreman rank the same jobs independently and then compare, which is the conversation two people who disagree about what to take on actually need.

    Is this only for contractors?

    No — it ranks any list where the items are hard to score but easy to compare two at a time. Jobs and quotes are the case it was built for, because a trade with more work than weeks is the person who most often has to choose. It works the same way on a feature backlog, a shortlist of suppliers, or a stack of quotes you are deciding which to chase first.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page. vs-scoring-every-job-out-of-ten.html.text:
← Which Job First?

This tool vs. scoring every job out of ten

Scoring a job list 1-10 feels rigorous, and usually comes back with three or four jobs clustered at the same number -- so the ranking still is not finished once the scoring is, and the tie gets broken by the same gut feel the scores were supposed to replace. This tool never asks for a number: it asks which of two jobs you would rather take, one pair at a time, and returns a complete order with nothing left to weigh.

What each approach actually does

Scoring out of ten asks you to convert an intuition into an absolute number with no fixed anchor, for every job on the list. Different jobs pull that number from different directions at once — urgency, pay, how much you dislike the client, drive time — and a 1-10 scale has far fewer distinct values than a typical job list has entries. Score twelve jobs and several will land on the same number, which means the hard part — deciding the order among the tied jobs — is still ahead of you, done by feel, after the scoring exercise that was supposed to replace feel.

This tool never asks for a score. It asks only which of two specific jobs you would rather take first — a comparison most people answer instantly and consistently — and runs a merge sort over your list, asking roughly n·log2(n) of those head-to-head questions before stopping with a complete order and no ties left over. The tradeoff it makes in exchange is assuming transitivity: if you prefer A to B and B to C, it never asks about A and C, and simply assumes you would also prefer A to C.

I want a number I can write on the job board next to each one.Scoring out of ten — this tool gives an order, not a score for each job.
I'm not sure my "urgency" score and my "pay" score should count the same.This tool — a pairwise pick already weighs everything you care about in one answer, with nothing to separately combine.
My jobs genuinely are not transitive (I'd take A over B, B over C, but C over A).Scoring out of ten — it does not need transitivity, since every job is judged against the same fixed scale rather than against each other.

Common questions

What is actually wrong with scoring each job out of ten?

Not the math -- the input. A score asks you to convert an intuition ("I'd rather do this one") into an absolute number with no anchor, and different jobs pull that number from different directions: urgency, pay, how much you dislike the client, drive time. Score twelve jobs and several will land on the same number, because a 1-10 scale has far fewer distinct values than a list of jobs usually has entries, so the ranking still isn't finished when the scoring is.

So what does this tool ask instead?

Only which of two specific jobs you would rather take first. That is a comparison most people can answer instantly and consistently, where a 1-10 score is a judgement call you can second-guess every time you revisit it. The tool runs a merge sort over your list, asking roughly n log2(n) of these head-to-head questions, and returns a complete order with no ties left over.

Is a pairwise comparison always better than a score?

No -- it assumes transitivity: if you prefer A to B and B to C, it never asks about A and C, and simply assumes you would also prefer A to C. A 1-10 score does not need that assumption, because every job is judged against the same fixed scale rather than against each other. For most short job lists transitivity holds well enough that the tradeoff favours fewer, easier questions; the tool's own guide says so rather than hiding the assumption.

Is my list uploaded anywhere?

No. The ranking runs entirely in your browser. Your job list, your answers, and the finished order are never uploaded, and the optional usage counter records only which features were used and the day -- never any job names or list contents.
